section_summary: This section traces Japan’s cotton industry from a 1932 market report through investigations of artificial cotton and staple fiber. Most of the pages are a 1936 illustrated statistical history of cotton imports, spinning, weaving, and warehousing. The final pages concern a 1939 cotton outlook report; the last memorandum continues beyond page 79.

subfiles.title: Document file note for Tokyo cotton telegram
subfiles.about: Cross-reference to a report on Japan’s cotton situation and industry.
subfiles.summary: Directs readers to section B of Neville’s March 23 telegram.

subfiles.title: Section B—Cotton
subfiles.about: Reports production, stocks, trade, and financial conditions in Japan’s cotton industry.
subfiles.summary: Cotton firms were generally profitable, aided by earlier low-priced purchases, but smaller firms faced difficulty. Yarn and textile exports were weakening, particularly because of conditions in China and British India.

subfiles.title: Request for information on artificial cotton
subfiles.from: Frederic D. Grab, Department of Commerce
subfiles.to: Assistant Secretary of State, attention A-C/C
subfiles.about: Requests an investigation and samples of wood-fiber artificial cotton reportedly developed in Kobe.
subfiles.summary: Asks the Kobe consul to verify the product and obtain samples.

subfiles.title: Production of Artificial Cotton in Japan
subfiles.about: Describes unsuccessful attempts to obtain samples and information on staple fiber.
subfiles.summary: Several Japanese rayon companies were preparing for production, but the product remained experimental and its process was guarded as a trade secret. Donovan expected market availability in late 1933 or early 1934.

subfiles.title: Division note on Kobe’s staple-fiber inquiry
subfiles.about: Summarizes the vice consul’s failed effort to learn about artificial cotton.
subfiles.summary: Concludes that Japanese sources guarded the material and further inquiries would be fruitless.

subfiles.title: Efforts to Obtain Samples of Artificial Cotton
subfiles.about: Forwards Vice Consul McConaughy’s memorandum on his inquiry into artificial cotton.
subfiles.summary: Encloses the November 17 account of an unsuccessful interview with a producer.

subfiles.title: Interview with Akira Yamauchi about staple fiber
subfiles.from: Walter P. McConaughy, American Vice Consul
subfiles.about: Records an interview with a prospective staple-fiber producer.
subfiles.summary: Yamauchi evaded questions and presented ordinary rayon as though it were the new fiber. McConaughy concluded that production details were closely guarded and further inquiries would be useless.

subfiles.title: Sample of Staple Fiber
subfiles.from: Kenneth C. Krentz, American Vice Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Forwards a staple-fiber sample for the Department of Commerce.
subfiles.summary: Reports that the Kobe consulate obtained and sent the requested sample.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of staple-fiber sample
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the sample and its referral for examination.
subfiles.summary: Conveys appreciation and says the Bureau of Standards will compare it with rayon.

subfiles.title: Division note on staple-fiber experiments
subfiles.about: Highlights a Kobe report on Japanese textile mills’ staple-fiber experiments.
subfiles.summary: Notes that leading mills were experimenting with the fiber as a wartime defense measure.

subfiles.title: Production of Staple Fiber in Japan
subfiles.about: Reassesses conflicting reports on Japanese staple-fiber production.
subfiles.summary: A British textile expert identified a sample as a wool substitute and described staple fiber as part of government contingency experiments. Donovan relayed the expert’s doubts about claims of imminent commercial production and warned that further local investigation would be unwise.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Consulate General letter on staple fiber
subfiles.from: Arthur Garrels, American Consul General, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Responds to Kobe’s questions about a reported Fuji Gas staple-fiber mill.
subfiles.summary: Tokyo says a company official largely confirmed the newspaper report, though the mill site was unsettled. It notes discrepancies with Kobe’s account and sends samples secured from another manufacturer.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of 25 Years of Cotton in Japan
subfiles.from: Kenneth C. Krentz, American Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Sends copies of U. A. Casal’s cotton-industry reference brochure.
subfiles.summary: Requests distribution to Agriculture, Commerce, and the Tariff Commission.

subfiles.title: 25 Years of Cotton in Japan
subfiles.from: U. A. Casal, F. S. Morse
subfiles.about: Compiles statistics, charts, photographs, and historical notes on Japan’s cotton trade from 1910 to 1935.
subfiles.summary: The brochure charts changes in raw-cotton imports by origin and port, the growth of spinning companies, yarn production, weaving, and textile exports. It discusses Osaka’s central role in trade, port and warehouse improvements, and the history of cotton cultivation and imports. It includes a warehouse company’s testimonial and a history of F. S. Morse.

subfiles.title: Document file note for 1936 industry memorandum
subfiles.about: Cross-reference concerning a U.S. textile delegation to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Points to a memorandum on visiting U.S. cotton-textile leaders.

subfiles.title: Document file note for Osaka cotton report
subfiles.about: Cross-reference to information on American cotton in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Points to an Osaka report on American cotton and Japan’s cotton industry.

subfiles.title: Corrected Pages for Japan Cotton Situation—Review and Outlook
subfiles.from: George A. Makinson, American Consul General, Osaka
subfiles.about: Transmits corrected replacement pages for a September 1939 cotton report.
subfiles.summary: Three significant typographical errors were found after urgent mailing; the despatch sends corrected pages 14 and 17 and table 12.

subfiles.title: Agriculture Department commendation of Osaka cotton report
subfiles.from: L. A. Wheeler, Office of Foreign Agricultural Relations
subfiles.about: Praises McConaughy’s Japan cotton outlook report.
subfiles.summary: Says the report and Osaka’s monthly information aid Agriculture’s annual outlook work.

subfiles.title: Routing slip for Japan Cotton Situation—Review and Outlook
subfiles.about: Records distribution of the cotton situation report.
subfiles.summary: Designates two copies for Agriculture.

subfiles.title: Routing slip for corrected pages
subfiles.about: Records distribution of corrected pages for the September cotton report.
subfiles.summary: Lists Commerce and Agriculture as recipients.

subfiles.title: Memorandum to Mr. Hornbeck on Japan Cotton Situation—Review and Outlook
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs; author unstated
subfiles.about: Highlights findings from McConaughy’s report on Japan’s 1938–39 cotton year.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes increased raw-cotton imports and cloth-export volume, alongside lower export value and weak prices. It discusses the changing origins of cotton, control measures, stocks, mill curtailment, the American export subsidy, wages, profits, and power shortages. Its discussion continues beyond page 79.
